fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The People Before the Greeks", "body": "Chance opens by defining the Pelasgi through Encyclopedia Britannica as the people who occupied Greece before the twelfth century BC, the era of the Bronze Age collapse and its baffling, intricate metalwork. Homer, Herodotus and Thucydides name them in Thrace, Argos, Crete and Chalcidice, and later Greek usage applied the label to every aboriginal Aegean population. Britannica adds that surviving fifth century villages preserved a common non-Greek language, a claim Dylan flatly calls disputable, alongside the admitted uncertainty that any ancient people ever called themselves by this name at all."}, {"title": "Sailors, Storks and Grasping Straws", "body": "Chance walks through competing origins for the name. Bishop Cumberland, writing in 1794, derived it from the Greek pelagos, the sea, reading it as a word for strangers and adventurers who came by ship to settle more comfortably. Marcellus of Lesbos tied it to storks that depart and return, an etymology Aristophanes mocked in a comedy of men dressed as birds. Godfrey Higgins doubted the sailors used the name themselves. William Betham instead read Celtic roots in the Iguvine tables, where night, light, day and people combine to mean navigators who could sail by darkness as well as daylight."}, {"title": "Baal, Aplu and Letter Swaps", "body": "Much of the argument happens at the whiteboard. Dylan spells Baal in Hebrew letters and insists the ayin carries the notation that begets the Greek omicron, so the name reads closer to Bel. Chance links that syllable to Homer's verb pello, to become or come into existence, and to the British deity Belenus. Dylan shows Etruscan Aplu written right to left, ties it to Apulia in the heel of Italy, and stresses that B, P and V trade places, that Castur and Puk are exclusive to Etruria, and that C worked as G before 230 BC."}, {"title": "Tyrrhenian Towers and One Source", "body": "Dylan argues the Tyrrhenian name came from the towers and forts these people built, and that Tyre was really Tsur, phonetically close to Syrian. Thracians reached as far as the Scythians, whose priests, the korybantes and kouretes, match those of the Umbrians and Etruscans, and whom he reads as remnants of trade routes running to the Black Sea. A Latin line stating that Etruscan, Phoenician and Celtic derive from one source was his checkmate. Academics, he says, force everything westward from Mesopotamia, when Etruscan salt beds, drained swampland and the Cloaca Maxima point to Italy."}, {"title": "Dorians, Druids and Darien", "body": "Chance traces the Dorians to Dora at the foot of Mount Lebanon in Phoenicia, then plays with dory, a small flat-bottomed boat, with the Old English dorre for tower, with the French word for tower, and with Spanish toro, the bull, which loops back to Baal and to the Taurus mountains. Herodotus calls those Phoenicians something close to Dorio, a short step to druid and to the tusci, the Etruscan priests. His strongest card is Lionel Wafer, stranded among the Darien tribe in the 1600s, who learned their speech within a month because the old Irish alphabet shared the same sixteen or seventeen letters."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: We are taught that Western civilization began with the Greeks, but the linguistic evidence reveals a much older, "secret" seafaring empire that was systematically erased from our history books.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In this remastered episode, we decode the "Ocean Language" of the Pelasgian, the Holy Sailors who mastered the Mediterranean and the Americas long before the Bronze Age collapse. By decoding the Hebrew and Phoenician roots hidden in plain sight, we reveal why the Pelasgians were the original 'Lordly' tribe mentioned in the oldest texts. Join Chance Garton and Dylan Saccoccio as they pull back the philological veil on the true architects of our world.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Metal, Salt and Drained Swamps", "body": "Dylan's case for Etruscan supremacy is material rather than mythic. They were exceptional with metalwork, he says, sitting on ore they could mine at home and on some of the best salt beds, at the mouth of the Tiber, which is what lifted them out of a nomadic life and into agriculture. They were also expert irrigators who drained swampland into farmland and pasture, and who cut the Cloaca Maxima long before Rome existed. Chance had not known about the drainage work, and Dylan points him to Etruscan filigree that nobody has since reproduced."}, {"title": "Did Anyone Reach the Americas", "body": "The Americas thread starts with Chance on terra preta, the ancient biochar technique he says makes rainforest soil so potent, and on his wondering whether whoever left the colony that became the Darien tribe also terraformed the forest. Dylan will not follow him to Italy. He points to Scotland, where burning produced the toughest cement because something in the soil activates, and says any crossing looks like people from Britain, the Basque country or northwestern Europe. What unsettles him is Peruvian masonry mirroring Italian masonry so closely that one of the two, probably the Peruvian, looks like a forgery."}, {"title": "Sea Peoples From the Wrong Direction", "body": "Chance reads the status quo account of the Sea Peoples, a hypothesized seafaring group that struck Egypt and the eastern Mediterranean before and during the late Bronze Age collapse, roughly 1200 to 900 BC, with several of them traced to the Aegean, Sicily, Sardinia, Cyprus and western Anatolia. His reframe is that historians are only confused because they place the Phoenicians in the east to begin with. Dylan answers with the wolf: Lykos, the Lykeian Apollo, the wolf-headed Sury, the Hirpini priests who lived in wolf skins by raiding, Romulus at the teat, and Lupercalia."}, {"title": "Which Alphabet Came First", "body": "The longest argument in the members hour is over which alphabet is older. Chance works through Higgins on two ancient scripts, the Pelasgic or Arcadian one brought into Latium by Evander, and the Ionian or Cadmean one credited to Cadmus, then argues from the Hebrew QDM that Cadmus means before rather than Oriental, and that Kadmon carries the value 200, matching Reish, head and beginning, which makes the man mythical. Against Higgins deriving the sixteen Pelasgic letters from Sanskrit, the counter runs the other way: the simpler alphabet is the older one, and the artifacts back it."}, {"title": "Hyperborea and the Hard G", "body": "Dylan reads the Diodorus passage from his book on the holy sailors: an island in the ocean opposite the coast of Gaul, no smaller than Sicily, lying north, fruitful twice a year, where Latona was born and Apollo is venerated above every other god in a round temple, with a sacred city of harpers beside it. He takes it for Ireland or Britain and says nowhere else fits. Chance then turns the Gaulish epithet Granus, from grene meaning sun, into Cronus on a hard G, a move Dylan had never made and hands straight back to him."}]

fields.Plus Quotes JSON: [{"text": "Part of what makes the rainforest so exceptional is the terra preta, which is basically an agricultural technique of making ancient biochar and creating extremely potent soil.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "I don't think the Italians made it to the Americas. I could be wrong.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "One thing I learned from Higgins was that he thought that Cyclops, as an idea, was a corruption of the concept of the third eye rather than a one-eyed giant.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "I don't think that the symbolism with the wolf applies better to anywhere than Italy.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "A pelorus is a tool for maintaining the bearing of a sea vessel. It's like a simplified compass. It's said to be named for Pelorus, the pilot of Hannibal in 203 BC.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "I keep noticing that whatever they have, I can find it in Italy older.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "So the Irish and the Basque, who you would think would be connected because the Bay of Biscay is on the way to Ireland, so you'd figure they would be stopping there.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "It could be a clue that the founders came from somewhere else, like the West, to establish the Near Eastern colonies rather than the Near Eastern colonies going west to establish them.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "And the idea of it, Kana, is also giving up one's individual leanings for the sake of a group, to move in orderly fashion, to move as one, and that's what the stars do.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "Nowhere else is Hyperborea, if you're going to say it's north of Gaul. Unless you're going to talk about Finland or something, but it's too cold up there.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/0d1bec4c-36ec-4ba4-a1cb-9de0908b2433/Dylan-Saccoccio.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}]
fields.Quotes JSON: [{"text": "It's a concept that will really help you understand the overall shifting of pieces on the chessboard in the historical era that is so murky and concealed by the ancient authors.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "These are all one people centered probably in the middle of the Mediterranean, which would be Italy, makes a lot of sense. Makes everything click.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Once you're aware of these little techniques of transposition, everything starts to gel.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": ""}, {"text": "I think a lot of this is nonsense or just people grasping for straws. And the reason for that is these are all coming at later times than these cultures existed.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": ""}, {"text": "It might be an indication of the actual logos or the spirit of wisdom coming through our language and trying to tell us who we are or wake us up.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "It was in Latin, but when you translate it, it said the Etruscan, Phoenician, and Celtic languages are all related, derived from one source.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": ""}, {"text": "I think what you're looking at is what you think of as ancient Rome was actually the Etruscan empire and then it just morphing into whatever they call the Roman Empire.", "author": "Dylan Saccoccio", "portrait": ""}, {"text": "That pretty much demonstrates a clear evidence that the Pelasgi made it to the Americas and left at least one colony.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}]
